title: Continuous cocycles and the completed augmentation resolution
statement:
Let $\Lambda$ be a finite commutative ring, $G$ a profinite group, and $M$ a discrete $\Lambda$-module with continuous $\Lambda$-linear $G$-action [def-exc-continuous-cohomology]. Define $A=\Lambda[[G]]=\varprojlim_{U\trianglelefteq_o G}\Lambda[G/U]$, with augmentation $\epsilon:A\to\Lambda$ summing coefficients, and put $I=\ker\epsilon$. Write $\operatorname{Hom}_{A,\mathrm{cont}}(I,M)$ for continuous $A$-linear maps, with $I$ carrying its subspace topology. A continuous crossed homomorphism is a continuous map $c:G\to M$ with $c(gh)=c(g)+g c(h)$; its coboundaries are $c_m(g)=gm-m$. Then there is a natural isomorphism
$$H^1_{\mathrm{cont}}(G,M)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{A,\mathrm{cont}}(I,M)\big/\{a\mapsto am:m\in M\},$$
which sends the class of $c$ to the class of the unique continuous $A$-linear map $f_c$ satisfying $f_c(g-1)=c(g)$ for every $g\in G$. This is the comparison with the augmented resolution $0\to I\to A\to\Lambda\to0$; in particular, whenever this resolution is used to compute degree one, it is this comparison, not its negative. If $\sigma$ topologically generates $G$ and $A\to I$, $a\mapsto a(1-\sigma)$, is a topological $A$-module isomorphism, all $A$-linear maps $I\to M$ are continuous and the same comparison identifies degree one with the cokernel of $M\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,M)$, $m\mapsto(a\mapsto am)$. In these coordinates
$$f_c(1-\sigma)=-c(\sigma).$$

source.place: Expose XVII, sections 1.2.1–1.2.2, augmentation-ideal resolution underlying the supported-cohomology model; continuous crossed-cocycle comparison and its sign are the agent-stated degree-one refinement. Standard cocycle relation is written explicitly in the statement.

proof.text: First make the finite coefficient constructions explicit. By [lem-exc-coinduced-functions-open-stabilizer], every continuous map $t:G\to S$ to a discrete space is constant on right cosets of some open normal $U$. Such a quotient $G/U$ is finite: its open cosets cover compact $G$, so finitely many cover it. Thus $t(G)$ is finite. Apply this also to the continuous orbit maps $g\mapsto gm$ for the finitely many $m$ in any finite subset $E\subset M$. The union of these finite orbits is finite and $G$-stable. Its $\Lambda$-span $N$ is finite, being the image of $\Lambda^r$ for a finite number $r$ of generators, and is $G$-stable. For every $n\in N$, apply the same cited statement to $g\mapsto gn$, and intersect the resulting finitely many open normal subgroups. The intersection acts trivially on $N$ (evaluate each orbit map at $1$). Consequently every finite subset of $M$ lies in a finite stable $N$ whose action factors through a finite quotient. Here only the coset factorization is a non-elementary input; the finite span and finite intersection are the displayed finite constructions.

source.place: Tag 04JP, definition-G-module-continuous; profinite coset factorization as stated in the cited node. Agent finite-span argument, using finite Lambda.

proof.text: For clarity the $A$-action on $M$ used in the statement is the following construction. Given $m$, choose $N$ and $U$ as in Step 1, let $Q=G/U$, and set $am=a_Um$ using the finite group-ring action on $N$, where $a_U\in\Lambda[Q]$ is the projection of $a$. This is independent of $N,U$: enlarge two choices to their sum and replace their subgroups by the intersection, then both formulas are the same finite sum of coefficients acting on $m$. Computing on a common finite stable submodule containing the finitely many vectors in question proves $(ab)m=a(bm)$, distributivity and $1m=m$. The orbit map $A\to M$, $a\mapsto am$, factors through the finite discrete ring $\Lambda[Q]$, hence is continuous. The same formula shows that a $G$-equivariant $\Lambda$-linear coefficient map commutes with the $A$-action.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1.1, pp. 259–260: completed group ring and discrete modules. Explicit finite-quotient construction supplied by the agent.

proof.text: Let $c:G\to M$ be a continuous crossed homomorphism. Step 1 gives finite image and a finite stable submodule $N$ containing it. Apply [lem-exc-coinduced-functions-open-stabilizer] to $c$, then intersect its open normal subgroup with one acting trivially on $N$ from Step 1. Write $U$ for this intersection, $Q=G/U$, and $\bar c:Q\to N$ for the resulting function. Normality makes $Q$ a group, and both the action and $c$ descend, so $\bar c(qr)=\bar c(q)+q\bar c(r)$. Also $c(1)=0$, by the cocycle identity at $(1,1)$. All statements below use this one common quotient, not a quotient that merely fixes one vector.

source.place: Tag 04JP, definition-G-module-continuous; apply the cited coset factorization to c and use the finite constructions in Step 1.

proof.text:
Define a $\Lambda$-linear map $L:\Lambda[Q]\to N$ by $L(\sum_q b_q q)=\sum_q b_q\bar c(q)$. For $q\in Q$ and $x=\sum_r b_r r$, the cocycle identity gives
$$L(qx)=qL(x)+\epsilon(x)\bar c(q).$$
Thus $L(qx)=qL(x)$ if $x\in I_Q:=\ker(\Lambda[Q]\xrightarrow\epsilon\Lambda)$; summing over $q$ shows that $L|_{I_Q}$ is $\Lambda[Q]$-linear. The projection $p_U:I\to I_Q$ therefore gives the continuous $A$-linear map $f_c=L\circ p_U:I\to N\hookrightarrow M$. Continuity follows from the finite discrete intermediary, and $A$-linearity from the action constructed in Step 2. Finally $f_c(g-1)=\bar c(\bar g)-\bar c(1)=c(g)$. This constructs the required map; no universal property of a completed free module is assumed.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1.1, pp. 259–260. Agent finite-sum construction of the degree-one comparison.

proof.text: The $\Lambda$-span $D$ of all $g-1$ is dense in $I$. Indeed a basic neighbourhood in the inverse limit prescribes finitely many quotient coordinates; replace their subgroups by their intersection $V$. If $a\in I$ has coordinate $a_V=\sum_{q\in G/V} b_q q$, then $\sum_q b_q=0$. Choose representatives $g_q\in G$. The element $\sum_q b_q(g_q-1)\in D$ has coordinate $a_V$, and hence matches all the prescribed coordinates. If two continuous $\Lambda$-linear maps $I\to M$ agree on $D$, their difference is zero everywhere: a nonzero value would, by continuity to discrete $M$, have a nonempty open fibre disjoint from dense $D$. This proves uniqueness of $f_c$, independence of the choices in Steps 3–4, and $\Lambda$-linearity of $c\mapsto f_c$, by checking each identity on $g-1$.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1.1: inverse-limit topology. Agent density and uniqueness argument in finite quotient coordinates.

proof.text:
Conversely, for continuous $A$-linear $f:I\to M$ put $c_f(g)=f(g-1)$. The map $g\mapsto g-1$ is continuous since each finite quotient coordinate is, and
$gh-1=(g-1)+g(h-1)$ implies $c_f(gh)=c_f(g)+gc_f(h)$. Thus $c_f$ is a continuous crossed homomorphism. Step 4 gives $c_{f_c}=c$, and Step 5 gives $f_{c_f}=f$, since both sides agree on $g-1$. For $m\in M$ the map $r_m:I\to M$, $x\mapsto xm$, is continuous by Step 2 and $A$-linear by associativity. Its corresponding cocycle is $c_{r_m}(g)=(g-1)m=gm-m$. Therefore the two inverse linear maps carry precisely the submodules of principal maps and coboundaries onto each other.

source.place: Tag 0DVG, section-continuous-group-cohomology: displayed degree-zero and degree-one differentials. Agent algebraic inverse and boundary computation.

proof.text:
Use the continuous inhomogeneous cochain model in [def-exc-continuous-cohomology]. Its differentials in degrees zero and one are
$$d^0m(g)=gm-m,\qquad d^1c(g,h)=gc(h)-c(gh)+c(g).$$
Hence its degree-one cohomology is exactly the quotient of continuous crossed homomorphisms by these coboundaries. Step 6 descends to the asserted isomorphism with $\operatorname{Hom}_{A,\mathrm{cont}}(I,M)/\{r_m\}$. For a continuous $G$-equivariant $\Lambda$-linear map $u:M\to M'$, $u f_c$ and $f_{uc}$ agree on every $g-1$, so Step 5 identifies them. This proves naturality in the coefficient module.

source.place: Tag 0DVG, section-continuous-group-cohomology, displayed inhomogeneous differential; the equivalence with the derived definition is explicitly part of the cited statement.

proof.text:
Check the augmentation comparison and its sign on the bar model [lem-sfb-bar-resolution-cochains]. Write $R=\mathbf Z[G]$. The ring map $R\to A$ sends each $g$ to its compatible quotient coordinates and each integer to its scalar in $\Lambda$. Define $R$-linear maps $\phi_0:B_0=R\to A$ by this ring map and $\phi_1:B_1\to I$ by $[g]\mapsto g-1$. Augmentations commute. The cited differential gives $d_1[g]=g-1$ and $d_2[g|h]=g[h]-[gh]+[g]$. Thus $\phi_0d_1$ equals inclusion composed with $\phi_1$, while
$$\phi_1d_2[g|h]=g(h-1)-(gh-1)+(g-1)=0.$$
Together with zero maps in higher degrees this is a chain map to $[I\hookrightarrow A]$. Precomposition in degrees zero and one sends $m$ to the same $m$ and $f$ to the cochain $g\mapsto f(g-1)$, exactly the map of Step 6. Restricting to continuous cochains is legitimate here because Step 6 proves this function continuous; no claim that abstract group cohomology equals continuous cohomology is used. The bijection of Step 6 proves that this restricted degree-one comparison is an isomorphism. This describes the comparison whenever the augmented complex computes degree one, without claiming that $I$ is projective for arbitrary $G$. In particular its inverse sends $[c]$ to $[f_c]$, not to $[-f_c]$.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2: augmentation complex. Agent explicit comparison with the signed bar differential stated in the cited Mathlib leaf.

proof.text: Now impose the additional topological $A$-module isomorphism $\theta:A\xrightarrow\sim I$, $a\mapsto a(1-\sigma)$. For an arbitrary algebraic $A$-linear map $f:I\to M$, set $m=f(1-\sigma)$. Then $(f\theta)(a)=am$, whose continuity was established in Step 2. Since $\theta^{-1}$ is continuous, $f=(f\theta)\theta^{-1}$ is continuous. The same argument identifies algebraic $\operatorname{Hom}_A(A,M)$ with $M$ by evaluation at $1$, and restriction along $I\hookrightarrow A$ sends $m$ precisely to $r_m$. Thus the degree-one quotient in Step 7 is the stated cokernel using all algebraic maps $I\to M$.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1.2 and 1.2.2, p. 260; the topological isomorphism is a hypothesis of the item, not an assertion proved here.

proof.text:
Finally $1-\sigma=-(\sigma-1)$, so the constructed comparison gives
$$f_c(1-\sigma)=-f_c(\sigma-1)=-c(\sigma).$$
For a coboundary this is $r_m(1-\sigma)=(1-\sigma)m=-(\sigma m-m)$, consistent with the same differential and quotient. This also checks the sign when $M$ has trivial action; in characteristic two the two signs coincide.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1.2 and 1.2.3, p. 260: coordinate 1-sigma. Agent sign check against the positive bar differential.
